title: Redis
subtitle: Single-threaded event loop architecture, core data structures, RDB vs AOF persistence, and Redis Cluster 16,384 hash slots.
keyTakeaways: Redis delivers 100k+ ops/sec via a single-threaded event loop paired with non-blocking I/O multiplexing (`epoll`), eliminating mutex lock contention.
Beyond simple key-value strings, Redis provides specialized in-memory data structures: Sorted Sets (`ZSET` skip-lists for leaderboards and rate limiters), Hashes, Bitmaps, and HyperLogLogs.
Redis Cluster partitions state into 16,384 CRC16 hash slots across master nodes without a central proxy layer, requiring `{hash_tag}` grouping for multi-key atomicity.

sections.heading: The Single-Threaded Architecture and Data Structure Mechanics
sections.body: Executing commands sequentially on a single thread simplifies concurrency: operations are naturally atomic without needing mutex locks. The flip side is operational vulnerability. If an engineer runs `KEYS *` or an unindexed Lua script that takes 500ms to process, Redis stops servicing every other connection for half a second. Client connection pools time out, health checks fail, and services cascade.
bullets: Sorted Sets (`ZSET`): Combines a Hash Table (O(1) lookups by element) with a Skip List (O(log N) range queries by score). Essential for sliding-window rate limiters, priority queues, and real-time leaderboards.

HyperLogLog: Approximates unique cardinality (like daily unique visitors) with a fixed 12 KB memory footprint and a 0.81% error margin, regardless of whether you track 1,000 or 100,000,000 unique IDs.

Pipelining vs Lua: Pipelining batches multiple independent commands into a single network socket write to eliminate round-trip latency; Lua scripts run multi-step read-modify-write logic atomically on the Redis server without network round trips.

sections.heading: Persistence Trade-offs (RDB vs AOF) and Cluster Topologies
sections.body: When using Redis for state that cannot be easily recomputed from SQL databases (such as rate-limiting windows or active user sessions), durability and clustering become critical design choices.
bullets: RDB Point-in-Time Snapshots: Periodically forks a child process using Linux Copy-on-Write (CoW) to stream memory pages to a compact binary dump on disk. Restarts are rapid, but crashes lose all data written between snapshot intervals.

Append-Only File (AOF): Logs every mutating command sequentially. Running with `appendfsync everysec` limits data loss to at most 1 second with negligible latency overhead. Redis 7+ combines an RDB snapshot base with an incremental AOF log for fast crash recovery.

Redis Cluster & Hash Tags: Smart clients hash keys via `CRC16(key) % 16384` and route directly to the owning master node. When running multi-key operations or transactions, enclose the sharding token in curly braces (e.g. `{user_123}:cart` and `{user_123}:profile`) to guarantee both keys land on the same node.

tradeOffs.pros: Minimal runtime disk I/O overhead; compact storage files; fastest recovery and restart times.
tradeOffs.cons: Data written between snapshot intervals is lost on unexpected process or host crashes.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Pure cache layers where data can be lazily reloaded from backing databases.

tradeOffs.pros: Limits potential data loss to a strict 1-second window; append-only format avoids corruption.
tradeOffs.cons: Larger disk footprint and background disk rewrite overhead during peak write traffic.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Session stores, rate limiters, write-behind buffers, and real-time state machines.
